title: Fully God, fully human
hookLine: the councils said: not half and half, but both at once

cards: Blue paint and yellow paint, stirred together, make green: something new, but no longer really blue or yellow. Tell a curious ten-year-old that Jesus is God and human, and that's often where the mind goes. So he's a mix?
Half God, half human, like a hero from the old Greek myths? Or maybe he's really God, and the human part is a sort of costume. Or really a man, a very holy one, and God sort of lives in him.
Someone in the early centuries taught a version of each, and each was turned down. Today's word is the answer the church gave instead, and it's stranger than any of them.

teach.b: In 451, at Chalcedon, the council from day two hundred eighty-three, bishops wrote a careful statement. Christ, they said, is one person, fully God and fully human. Truly God, of one being with the Father.

Truly human, with a body and a human mind and soul, like us in everything except sin. And the two natures are joined without being mixed, without being changed, without being divided, without being separated.
Four withouts, and each one closes a door. Not mixed: he's not green paint. Not changed: God doesn't stop being God, and the human doesn't dissolve.
Not divided or separated: he isn't two people sharing one body; he's one person, one who. Why did it matter?

teach.h: WHAT HE DIDN'T TAKE ON, HE DIDN'T HEAL.
teach.b: Recall yesterday's line, as a bishop named Gregory of Nazianzus put it, roughly: whatever of us he didn't take on, he didn't heal. If Jesus had no real human mind, our minds aren't healed.
If he wasn't truly God, it isn't God who came close.
The churches hold it as a mystery, not a puzzle to solve.
The ancient churches of the east, from day two hundred eighty-four, put it in different words, one united nature, but they too say fully God and fully human.

Look back at this week: Pentecostals and the Spirit; what the churches share; the creed; the Maker of heaven and earth; the Trinity; the Word made flesh; and today, both at once. A week on who God is, and who Jesus is.

how: Christians confess Jesus as fully God and fully human in the Nicene Creed and in hymns, and many Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, which names him Lord and Son of God.

games.q: Chalcedon, 451. one teacher says Christ's divine and human natures blended into something new. another says they're two people in one body. what does the council say?
o: one person, two natures, without mixing and without dividing.
games.why: the council turned both down: one person, fully God and fully human, without being mixed, changed, divided or separated.

practice: Hold two true things in mind at once: about yourself, that you're fragile and strong, or about someone you love, that they drive you crazy and you'd do anything for them. Don't blend them; let both be fully true.
If you pray, hold before God the mystery of Christ, fully God and fully human; if you don't, stay with your two truths.

wordCard.voice: Fully God. The church's claim at Chalcedon: Jesus is fully God and fully human, one person, both at once, not half and half.

orig.note: Greek: what stands under. At Chalcedon, the one person in whom the two natures meet.

carryVoice: Your line: both at once. Not half and half, and not green paint. Day three hundred one.
